title: Titus Andronicus
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Imperial Rome and the forest outside it, at no identifiable date
lengthNote: Around 2,500 lines, of which the opening scene alone takes nearly 500
openingLine: Noble patricians, patrons of my right, Defend the justice of my cause with arms
summary: A general comes home from ten years of war, buries his sons, and sacrifices a captive prince to their spirits because Roman piety requires it. The prince’s mother becomes empress within the hour, and the rest of the play is her repayment: a son-in-law murdered, a daughter raped and maimed, two sons beheaded on false evidence, and a hand cut off for nothing. Shakespeare’s first tragedy is not shapeless. It is a machine, and its subject is what a city calls justice once revenge has learnt to wear the forms of law.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Titus Andronicus
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which includes the fly scene (3.2) found only in the Folio. Modern editions vary by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Probably Shakespeare’s first tragedy, and possibly written with George Peele, whom many attribute the opening act to.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The first Shakespeare play ever to reach print. A single copy of the quarto survives, in the Folger Library.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: Lavinia’s fate follows Philomela in the Metamorphoses; the banquet follows Seneca’s Thyestes. There is no historical Titus.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I is one continuous scene in which an emperor is chosen, a prince sacrificed, a son killed by his father and a bride stolen.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A triumph, a sacrifice and a wedding, all before the tomb is shut
structure.summary: Two brothers contest the empire; Titus returns with Gothic prisoners and gives the crown to the elder, Saturninus. He has Tamora’s eldest son hacked to pieces for his dead sons’ sake, kills his own son Mutius for obstructing him, and loses Lavinia to Bassianus anyway. Saturninus marries Tamora instead, and she promises, aside, to massacre the whole family.

scenes.title: Rome chooses
scenes.summary: Saturninus is made emperor on Titus’s word; Alarbus is sacrificed; Mutius dies; Tamora becomes empress and plans her revenge.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The hunt
structure.summary: Aaron, Tamora’s lover, redirects her sons’ quarrel over Lavinia into a plan for the forest. In a pit Aaron has prepared, Bassianus is murdered and two of Titus’s sons are framed for it with a forged letter. Chiron and Demetrius rape Lavinia and cut out her tongue and hands so that she cannot name them. Her uncle Marcus finds her and speaks for forty lines before he can lead her home.

scenes.title: Aaron’s plan
scenes.summary: Aaron turns the brothers’ rivalry for Lavinia into a shared plot for the hunt.

scenes.title: The morning of the hunt
scenes.summary: Titus greets the emperor with hounds and horns.

scenes.title: The pit
scenes.summary: Bassianus is killed, Lavinia is dragged away, and Quintus and Martius are found in the pit with the body.

scenes.title: Marcus finds Lavinia
scenes.summary: Chiron and Demetrius mock the woman they have mutilated; Marcus tries to read her in Ovid’s terms.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The hand
structure.summary: Titus pleads to tribunes who walk past him, then to the stones. Lucius is banished, Lavinia is brought in, and Aaron arrives with an offer: a hand for the lives of the two condemned sons. Titus cuts his off, and a messenger returns it with the sons’ heads. He laughs, and sends Lucius to the Goths. In the Folio’s added scene, the family dine and Marcus kills a fly.

scenes.title: The plea and the hand
scenes.summary: Titus pleads to the street, loses a hand, receives two heads, and stops weeping.

scenes.title: The fly
scenes.summary: At table, Titus resolves to learn Lavinia’s signs, then mourns a fly until he hears it was black.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Reading, writing and arrows
structure.summary: Lavinia turns the pages of a copy of Ovid to the story of Philomela and, holding a staff in her mouth, writes the names of her attackers in the sand. Tamora’s baby is born black and Aaron kills the nurse to protect him. Titus has his kinsmen shoot petitions to the gods over the palace walls, and a clown carrying his message is hanged for it.

scenes.title: The book
scenes.summary: Lavinia finds the tale of Philomel and writes ‘Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.’ in the sand.

scenes.title: The child
scenes.summary: Aaron refuses to kill his black son, kills the nurse instead, and takes the baby to the Goths.

scenes.title: Arrows
scenes.summary: Titus, saying Astraea has left the earth, shoots letters to the gods.

scenes.title: The clown
scenes.summary: Saturninus rages at the arrows; the clown is hanged; news comes that Lucius marches on Rome with the Goths.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Revenge comes to dinner
structure.summary: Aaron is captured with his child and confesses everything with relish. Tamora, dressed as Revenge with her sons as Rape and Murder, visits Titus to trick him; he recognises her, keeps the sons, and cuts their throats while Lavinia holds the basin. At the banquet he serves them to their mother in a pie, kills Lavinia, kills Tamora, is killed by Saturninus, who is killed by Lucius. Lucius is made emperor and orders Aaron buried to the chest and Tamora thrown to the birds.

scenes.title: Aaron’s confession
scenes.summary: Captured by Lucius, Aaron bargains for his child’s life with the whole history of the plot.

scenes.title: Revenge, Rape and Murder
scenes.summary: Tamora’s masque fails; Titus binds her sons and butchers them.

scenes.title: The banquet
scenes.summary: The pie, four deaths in a dozen lines, and Lucius’s settlement of the state.

characters.name: Titus Andronicus
characters.role: Roman general, father of twenty-five sons and one daughter
characters.summary: He has buried twenty-one sons for Rome and treats piety as a set of procedures: sacrifice, burial, obedience to the elder claimant. The procedures produce his own destruction, and the play watches him learn a different language, first grief’s and then Revenge’s, with the same literal-mindedness he brought to the first.
characters.clue: He kills one son for blocking a doorway, cuts off his own hand to save two more, and cooks the men who hurt his daughter.

relationships.label: sacrifices her son, is destroyed by, kills

characters.name: Lavinia
characters.summary: Married in the first scene, widowed, raped and mutilated in the second act, she spends the rest of the play being interpreted by men who cannot stop describing her. Her one act of authorship is a Latin word and two names written with a stick, and it is the only piece of evidence in the play that is true.
characters.clue: She turns the pages of Ovid with her stumps and writes three words in the sand with a staff held in her mouth.

characters.name: Tamora
characters.role: Queen of the Goths, then empress of Rome
characters.summary: She enters a prisoner and pleads for her son in the play’s best argument about mercy; when it fails, she never argues again. Her revenge is more patient than Titus’s and better disguised, and in the last act she overreaches by turning it into theatre, playing Revenge to a man who knows exactly who she is.
characters.clue: She begs for mercy for her first-born, is refused, and becomes empress before the scene is over.

characters.name: Aaron
characters.role: A Moor, Tamora’s lover and the plot’s engineer
characters.summary: He designs the pit, the forged letter, the rape and the bargain for the hand, and takes credit for all of it in a confession he clearly enjoys. He is also the only parent in the play who will not sacrifice a child. Rome’s language for him is entirely about colour, and he answers it with the play’s one speech in praise of being black.
characters.clue: He kills a nurse to keep a baby alive, and regrets only the ten thousand crimes he never had time for.

characters.name: Saturninus
characters.role: Elder son of the late emperor, made emperor by Titus
characters.summary: He is given the empire and resents the giver within fifty lines. Weak, jealous and quick to believe whatever evidence is put in front of him, he is the reason Aaron’s plots work: the forged letter and the bodies in the pit convince him because he wants them to.
characters.clue: Handed a crown by the man whose daughter he then abandons for a captive queen, he later hangs a clown for delivering a letter.

characters.name: Lucius
characters.summary: He demands the sacrifice of Alarbus in the first scene and inherits Rome in the last, which is the play’s bleakest joke about restoration. Banished, he returns at the head of the Goths, the people his father spent ten years fighting, and the settlement he announces begins with two more punishments.
characters.clue: Banished for trying to rescue his brothers, he comes back leading the enemy army and ends the play as emperor.

characters.name: Marcus Andronicus
characters.role: Tribune of the people, Titus’s brother
characters.summary: The family’s civilian, who offers Titus the empire and spends the rest of the play trying to make grief articulate. His long speech over the mutilated Lavinia is either the play’s worst lapse of taste or its most honest moment, depending on whether you think eloquence can be a form of shock.
characters.clue: A tribune who finds his niece in the forest and, having no idea what to do, compares her to Philomela for forty lines.

characters.name: Chiron and Demetrius
characters.summary: They quarrel over Lavinia like schoolboys until Aaron shows them they need not choose. After the rape they taunt her to call for water and are never intelligent again: they miss the meaning of a Latin tag, of a bundle of weapons wrapped in a verse, and finally of an old man asking them to sit down to dinner.
characters.clue: Two brothers who wrap a rape in a hunting party, and end the play as a pastry.

characters.name: Bassianus
characters.role: The late emperor’s younger son, Lavinia’s husband
characters.summary: He loses the election, seizes his betrothed by force of arms, and is murdered in the forest for taunting the empress about her lover. He is on stage for two scenes and his body is the evidence that hangs two innocent men.
characters.clue: He claims his bride at sword-point in the first scene and is a corpse in a pit by the second act.

themes.name: Revenge as a form
themes.summary: Nobody in this play takes revenge in hot blood. Tamora waits four acts; Titus waits until he has been handed the perfect shape for it by his enemy’s own masque. Revenge here is a genre with rules — a pit, a letter, a banquet — and each side is trying to be the better author of it.
themes.development: A sacrifice in Act I is answered by a rape in Act II, a hand in Act III by a confession in Act V, and the final banquet answers everything at once.

themes.name: Justice that has left the earth
themes.summary: Titus says it in Latin in 4.3: Astraea, goddess of justice, has abandoned the world. Rome’s courts condemn two sons on a forged letter and hang a clown for carrying a petition, so the only justice available is the private kind, and the play does not pretend that the private kind is any better.
themes.development: Tamora pleads for mercy and gets none; Titus pleads to tribunes who walk past him; by Act V he has stopped pleading and started cooking.

themes.name: Bodies as evidence
themes.summary: What people believe in this Rome depends on what has been arranged for them to see. The bodies in the pit convict Quintus and Martius; the heads sent back to Titus prove the emperor’s word is worthless; Lavinia’s body is a text that everybody reads and nobody, until Ovid, can construe.
themes.development: Aaron’s forged letter is the first false document; Lavinia’s three words in the sand are the first true one, and they arrive two acts later.

themes.name: Speech, silence and the tongue
themes.summary: Lavinia has her tongue cut out so that she cannot accuse, and the play then becomes obsessed with what a person without speech can still say. Marcus’s wish that he could read her heart, Titus’s promise to wrest an alphabet from her gestures, and the book of Ovid are three attempts to give a voice back to someone the plot has silenced.
themes.development: In 2.4 she cannot speak; in 3.2 she will be interpreted; in 4.1 she writes; in 5.3 her father kills her so that the shame will not outlive him.

themes.name: Aaron and the language of colour
themes.summary: Rome cannot mention Aaron without mentioning his colour, and the insult is so constant that it becomes a structure of the play rather than a detail. His speech on the child, ‘coal-black is better than another hue’, is the only time anyone in Rome argues back, and it is the only defence of a child that the play contains.
themes.development: In Act II he is ‘the Moor’; in 4.2 he becomes a father and turns the vocabulary round; in 5.3 he is buried alive still refusing to say the word ‘repent’.

themes.name: Roman honour and piety
themes.summary: Titus is not a monster in the first scene; he is a Roman doing the correct things. Sacrifice for the dead, the tomb, obedience to the elder son, the killing of a son who disobeys: each act is pious by the standards Rome has taught him, and each sets the machine going. The play asks what piety is worth when it produces this.
themes.development: The first scene stages honour as ceremony; by Act IV honour has become arrows shot at heaven; at the end Lucius rebuilds the state with two more executions.

techniques.name: Allusion
techniques.definition: Quotation or reference used to enlarge, or to puncture, the scene at hand.
techniques.inThisBook: Ovid’s Philomela, Seneca’s Thyestes and Virgil’s Aeneas are named on stage, and Lavinia’s attackers are identified because a schoolboy’s copy of the Metamorphoses is in the house. The classics are not decoration; they are the plot’s instruction manual.

techniques.name: Stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries far more weight than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: A severed hand carried off in Lavinia’s teeth, two heads in a bag, a staff held in the mouth, arrows wrapped in petitions, a basin for blood, a pie: the props are the play’s argument about what a body is worth.

techniques.name: Apostrophe
techniques.definition: Speech addressed to something that cannot answer.
techniques.inThisBook: Titus pleads to the tribunes, then to the stones in the street, then to the earth, then by arrow to the gods. Each address goes to a listener less able to reply than the last, which is how the play measures Rome’s deafness.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play drawing attention to the fact that it is a play.
techniques.inThisBook: Tamora arrives in costume as Revenge with her sons as Rape and Murder, and Titus plays along, correcting her casting. The revenger who was handed his own role by his enemy then stages a banquet with a cook’s hat on.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: For four acts the villains know more than the victims. In 5.2 the balance tips: Tamora thinks Titus is mad and Titus knows exactly who is under the mask, and the audience is finally on the side that knows.

techniques.name: Formal lament
techniques.definition: Grief set out as a patterned, extended speech rather than a cry, so that the ornament itself becomes part of what is felt.
techniques.inThisBook: Marcus’s speech over Lavinia in 2.4 and Titus’s ‘I am the sea’ in 3.1 are laments built from conceits, and the play tests how long such speech can go on before somebody laughs. Titus does, at 3.1.266.

quotations.text: Wilt thou draw near the nature of the gods? Draw near them then in being merciful: Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge: Thrice noble Titus, spare my first-born son.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Kneeling to Titus as Alarbus is chosen for sacrifice.
quotations.analysis: The argument is Portia’s, twenty years early, and it fails. Tamora reasons from the gods downward and ends with the plain word ‘son’, and Titus answers with ‘Patient yourself, madam’, which is the reply of a man who has not heard a word. Everything that follows is what happens to an argument for mercy that nobody in authority will listen to.

quotations.text: Was ever Scythia half so barbarous?
quotations.speaker: Chiron
quotations.context: As Alarbus is led away to be hewn and burnt; Demetrius answers ‘Oppose not Scythia to ambitious Rome.’
quotations.analysis: The Goth calls Rome barbarous, and his brother does not disagree: he says only that Rome is ambitious, which is worse. One line reverses the play’s whole geography of civilisation and savagery before the first act is a quarter done.

quotations.text: I'll find a day to massacre them all And raze their faction and their family, The cruel father and his traitorous sons, To whom I sued for my dear son's life
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Aside to Saturninus, while publicly urging him to be reconciled to the Andronici.
quotations.analysis: She is being merciful out loud and murderous in the aside, at the same moment, to the same husband. The play’s method is laid out here: revenge conducted through the forms of reconciliation, and a public face that means the opposite of what the audience hears.

quotations.text: Away with slavish weeds and servile thoughts! I will be bright, and shine in pearl and gold, To wait upon this new-made empress.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Alone, opening Act II, after Tamora has become empress.
quotations.analysis: His first soliloquy is about wardrobe. A captive plans to dress like a courtier, and the ambition is stated as light against dark, which is the vocabulary Rome will use against him for the rest of the play. He takes it up before they can.

quotations.text: She is a woman, therefore may be woo'd; She is a woman, therefore may be won; She is Lavinia, therefore must be loved.
quotations.speaker: Demetrius
quotations.context: Quarrelling with Chiron over who shall have Lavinia.
quotations.analysis: The syllogism is a schoolroom trick, and the third line breaks it: ‘must be loved’ is not a conclusion but a demand. Shakespeare reused the first two lines almost word for word in Henry VI, Part 1, which shows how far the sentiment is stock; what is new here is what the brothers do with it.

quotations.text: Vengeance is in my heart, death in my hand, Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Refusing Tamora’s invitation to make love in the forest.
quotations.analysis: Tamora has just described the forest as a place for Dido and Aeneas; Aaron replies with a body inventory in which every organ has been assigned a job. The couplet is nearly a stage direction, and it is the closest the play comes to a definition of its own genre.

quotations.text: Speak, gentle niece, what stern ungentle hands Have lopp'd and hew'd and made thy body bare Of her two branches, those sweet ornaments, Whose circling shadows kings have sought to sleep in
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Finding Lavinia in the forest after the rape.
quotations.analysis: He asks her to speak, knowing within a line that she cannot, and then does the speaking for her in a conceit that turns her arms into branches and her body into a tree. ‘Lopp’d and hew’d’ was Lucius’s phrase for what was done to Alarbus in 1.1: the play’s vocabulary of sacrifice has come home.

quotations.text: Shall I speak for thee? shall I say 'tis so? O, that I knew thy heart; and knew the beast, That I might rail at him, to ease my mind!
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Still addressing the mutilated Lavinia, having guessed at a rape.
quotations.analysis: The offer to speak for her is generous and also the problem: for three acts men will speak for Lavinia, and the ‘I’ in ‘to ease my mind’ admits whose relief the speaking serves. The play has noticed what its own eloquence is for.

quotations.text: Hear me, grave fathers! noble tribunes, stay! For pity of mine age, whose youth was spent In dangerous wars, whilst you securely slept
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Lying in the street as the judges lead his sons to execution.
quotations.analysis: The general who gave Rome its emperor now opens an act on the ground. The tribunes do not answer, and by the end of the speech he is addressing the stones, which he says are better listeners. Act III begins where Tamora’s plea ended in Act I, and on the same result.

quotations.text: Why, foolish Lucius, dost thou not perceive That Rome is but a wilderness of tigers? Tigers must prey, and Rome affords no prey But me and mine: how happy art thou, then, From these devourers to be banished!
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: To Lucius, who has just been sentenced to banishment for trying to rescue his brothers.
quotations.analysis: Banishment is congratulated as an escape, which inverts the whole Roman value of belonging. The tiger returns at the end of the play when Lucius calls Tamora ‘that heinous tiger’, and the audience is left to notice that the wilderness Titus describes now has an Andronicus on the throne.

quotations.text: For now I stand as one upon a rock Environed with a wilderness of sea, Who marks the waxing tide grow wave by wave
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: As Lavinia is brought before him for the first time since the rape.
quotations.analysis: ‘Wilderness’ was tigers forty lines ago and is now sea; the same word keeps being reached for because Titus has no other. The image is of a man watching disaster arrive in instalments, which is exactly the shape of the scene: two sons condemned, then a daughter maimed, then a hand, then two heads.

quotations.text: I am the sea; hark, how her sighs do blow! She is the weeping welkin, I the earth
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: After Marcus has begged him to stop weeping; Lavinia is beside him.
quotations.analysis: He answers a request for restraint by becoming a weather system. The conceit is so large that it contains the whole family — Lavinia is sky, Titus is sea and earth at once — and it is the last lament before the heads arrive and he laughs. The play sets the limit of grief-as-eloquence precisely here.

quotations.text: Why, I have not another tear to shed: Besides, this sorrow is an enemy, And would usurp upon my watery eyes And make them blind with tributary tears
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Marcus has asked why he laughed on being shown his sons’ heads and his own hand.
quotations.analysis: The laugh at 3.1.266 is the hinge of the play, and this is its explanation: sorrow is redefined as an enemy, which is the vocabulary of war, and eyes are needed for finding ‘Revenge’s cave’. From here Titus stops being the play’s chief sufferer and becomes its chief plotter.

quotations.text: Thou map of woe, that thus dost talk in signs!
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: At table with Lavinia, in the scene found only in the Folio.
quotations.analysis: A map is a surface to be read, and the line says plainly what the play has been doing to Lavinia since 2.4. ‘Talk in signs’ also concedes that she is talking: the fly scene is where Titus starts treating her gestures as a language rather than a spectacle.

quotations.text: Thou shalt not sigh, nor hold thy stumps to heaven, Nor wink, nor nod, nor kneel, nor make a sign, But I of these will wrest an alphabet And by still practise learn to know thy meaning.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: To Lavinia, promising to learn to read her gestures.
quotations.analysis: ‘Wrest’ is a violent verb for an act of love: he will force a language out of her the way the plot forced silence on her. The promise is kept in the next act, but not by Titus — it is Lavinia who finds the book, and the alphabet turns out to be Ovid’s.

quotations.text: O, why should nature build so foul a den, Unless the gods delight in tragedies?
quotations.speaker: Marcus
quotations.context: Lavinia has just pointed to the story of Philomela in Ovid, and Titus has guessed the place of the rape.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked inside a tragedy, by a character, about the gods as an audience, which makes it one of Shakespeare’s earliest jokes about the people watching. It also notices that the forest in Act II was designed: Aaron built the den, and the play built Aaron.

quotations.text: 'Stuprum. Chiron. Demetrius.'
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Reading aloud what Lavinia has written in the sand with a staff guided by her mouth and feet.
quotations.analysis: Three words, one of them Latin, and they are the first true testimony in a play full of forged letters and arranged bodies. The evidence that convicts is produced by the one person who cannot speak, in a language learnt from the book that also described her crime.

quotations.text: Villain, I have done thy mother.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: To Demetrius, who has just called the black baby a villain and drawn his sword on it.
quotations.analysis: Six words, and the play’s only pun that the villains understand. Aaron is answering an insult with a fact, and the fact is a father claiming a son. The line is often played for a laugh and it earns one, but what follows is the play’s single unconditional act of protection.

quotations.text: Coal-black is better than another hue, In that it scorns to bear another hue; For all the water in the ocean Can never turn the swan's black legs to white
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Defending his newborn son from Tamora’s order that the child be killed.
quotations.analysis: Rome’s word for him is ‘black’ and it is always an accusation; here he turns the word into a virtue by making it mean constancy. The swan is usually the emblem of whiteness, and the argument quietly points out that even a swan has black legs. It is the first speech in English drama to defend blackness on its own terms.

quotations.text: Terras Astraea reliquit: Be you remember'd, Marcus, she's gone, she's fled.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Handing out bows and arrows tipped with petitions to the gods.
quotations.analysis: The Latin is Ovid’s again: Astraea, justice, has left the earth. Titus quotes it as a matter of fact and then organises a search party, which is how the play handles madness — as a literal-minded response to a true statement. The arrows are the only appeal to a higher court that Rome still allows.

quotations.text: The eagle suffers little birds to sing, And is not careful what they mean thereby, Knowing that with the shadow of his wings He can at pleasure stint their melody
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Calming Saturninus, who is furious at the arrows and the clown’s message.
quotations.analysis: She counsels contempt for Titus’s petitions and is wrong: the little bird is about to bake her sons. The eagle is Rome’s bird, and the image gives her exactly the imperial confidence that will walk her into Titus’s house in costume two scenes later.

quotations.text: Tut, I have done a thousand dreadful things As willingly as one would kill a fly, And nothing grieves me heartily indeed But that I cannot do ten thousand more.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: Ending his confession to Lucius, the noose already prepared.
quotations.analysis: The fly is not idle: in 3.2 Titus wept for one until he was told it was black, then stabbed it twice. Aaron’s boast borrows the smallest death in the play to measure the largest number, and the arithmetic — a thousand done, ten thousand wanted — is a parody of Titus’s twenty-five sons.

quotations.text: I am Revenge: sent from the infernal kingdom, To ease the gnawing vulture of thy mind, By working wreakful vengeance on thy foes.
quotations.speaker: Tamora
quotations.context: Disguised, at Titus’s door, with her sons as Rape and Murder.
quotations.analysis: The empress plays an allegorical figure from a morality play to a man she believes is mad, and the man has already recognised her. The speech is the play describing its own genre out loud, and the audience watches the revenger’s enemy hand him the plot.

quotations.text: Why, there they are both, baked in that pie; Whereof their mother daintily hath fed, Eating the flesh that she herself hath bred.
quotations.speaker: Titus
quotations.context: Answering Saturninus’s demand that Chiron and Demetrius be fetched.
quotations.analysis: The reveal is a rhymed couplet and ‘daintily’ is the cruellest word in it. Seneca’s Thyestes ends with the same meal, but Shakespeare adds a stage direction Seneca could not: the mother is at the table, and the audience has watched her eat.

quotations.text: If one good deed in all my life I did, I do repent it from my very soul.
quotations.speaker: Aaron
quotations.context: His last words, sentenced to be buried breast-deep and starved.
quotations.analysis: Lucius has demanded repentance and Aaron supplies the form of it with the content reversed, which is exactly the trick Tamora played on mercy in Act I. He exits the play as its only character who never once said something he did not mean.

quotations.text: Then, afterwards, to order well the state, That like events may ne'er it ruinate.
quotations.speaker: Lucius
quotations.context: The last lines of the play, after ordering Tamora’s body thrown to the birds.
quotations.analysis: The promise of order comes after two sentences of punishment, from the man who demanded the sacrifice that started everything. The couplet rhymes ‘state’ with ‘ruinate’, and the audience is invited to weigh whether the new emperor has understood the word ‘like’.

timeline.label: Ovid’s Metamorphoses
timeline.detail: Completed around AD 8. Book VI tells of Philomela, raped by Tereus, silenced by the loss of her tongue, and avenged with a meal of his son.

timeline.label: Golding’s English Metamorphoses
timeline.detail: Arthur Golding’s complete translation put Ovid in English verse; Shakespeare’s Lavinia turns the pages of the Latin.

timeline.label: Seneca His Tenne Tragedies printed in English
timeline.detail: The collected translations made Thyestes, with its cannibal banquet, part of the Elizabethan stage’s inheritance.

timeline.label: First recorded performance and first printing
timeline.detail: Henslowe noted the play at the Rose on 24 January; John Danter entered it in the Stationers’ Register on 6 February and printed the quarto that year, the first Shakespeare play in print.

timeline.label: The Peacham drawing
timeline.detail: A manuscript at Longleat, usually dated around 1595, shows Tamora pleading before Titus and is the only contemporary illustration of a Shakespeare play in performance.

timeline.label: Second quarto
timeline.detail: Reprinted from the 1594 text; a third quarto followed in 1611.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Adds the fly scene, 3.2, which appears in no quarto.

timeline.label: Ravenscroft’s Titus Andronicus, or The Rape of Lavinia
timeline.detail: Edward Ravenscroft’s adaptation, with its preface doubting Shakespeare’s authorship, shaped the play’s reputation for over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook’s production at Stratford
timeline.detail: With Laurence Olivier as Titus and Vivien Leigh as Lavinia, Brook’s stylised staging is usually credited with rescuing the play for the modern theatre.

timeline.label: Deborah Warner at the Swan
timeline.detail: Brian Cox’s Titus in a small-scale, uncut production that let the play’s laughter and horror sit side by side.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor’s film Titus
timeline.detail: Anthony Hopkins and Jessica Lange in a version that mixes Roman ruins, Fascist design and modern dress.

places.name: Rome, the Capitol
places.note: The play opens before the Capitol, where the empire is contested and the Andronici’s tomb receives its dead.

places.name: The Rose, Bankside
places.note: Henslowe recorded the play here on 24 January 1594, the earliest performance we know of.

places.name: Longleat House, Wiltshire
places.note: Home of the Peacham manuscript, the one contemporary drawing of a Shakespeare play on stage.

places.name: Folger Shakespeare Library, Washington
places.note: Holds the only surviving copy of the 1594 quarto.

places.name: The Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Deborah Warner’s 1987 production, the modern benchmark for staging the play uncut.

criticalViews.summary: From Ravenscroft onward, the play was treated as juvenile, collaborative or not Shakespeare’s at all: a heap of atrocities strung on a Senecan frame, interesting mainly for what it anticipates in Lear and Othello.
criticalViews.counter: The structure is too controlled for the charge to stick. Every horror is answered by another in a pattern the characters themselves can read, and the fly scene shows a writer already interested in what grief does to language.

criticalViews.position: A play about reading and evidence
criticalViews.summary: Much recent criticism follows the props: the forged letter, the bodies in the pit, the book of Ovid, the words in the sand. On this view the play’s subject is how a state decides what counts as proof, and Lavinia is its central witness rather than its central victim.
criticalViews.counter: It can make the violence sound like a seminar. The play also wants the audience to flinch, and productions that forget this become tidy.

criticalViews.position: Aaron as the play’s honest man
criticalViews.summary: Readings attentive to race note that Aaron is the only character who says what he means, the only parent who protects a child, and the one against whom Rome’s language of colour is deployed without pause. His refusal to repent is read as integrity rather than villainy.
criticalViews.counter: He also designs the rape and the frame-up and says he enjoyed them. The play makes him more interesting than the Romans without making him better.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Titus is not a victim of Rome; he is its product.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Piety, ceremony and the first scene
plan: Begin with 1.1: every act of Titus’s — the sacrifice, the handing over of the crown, the killing of Mutius — is presented as correct Roman conduct.
Use Tamora’s plea for mercy to show the play offering an alternative and Rome refusing it.
Trace how the vocabulary of sacrifice (‘lopp’d and hew’d’) returns on Titus’s own family in Act II.
Consider Act III, where the tribunes ignore him as he ignored Tamora, and the laugh at 3.1.266.
Close on Lucius’s settlement: the new Rome begins with two punishments, and the cycle is not obviously broken.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play present Lavinia after the rape?
plan: Start with Marcus in 2.4: eloquence spent on a woman who cannot answer, and the question of whom that eloquence serves.
Set the fly scene’s ‘map of woe’ and the promise to wrest an alphabet against her own act of writing in 4.1.
Argue that the play distinguishes between being read and testifying, and that Lavinia does both.
Consider her part in 5.2, holding the basin, as either participation or further use.
Weigh her death at Titus’s hands: mercy, shame, or the last act of speaking for her.

essayQuestions.question: Is Aaron the villain of Titus Andronicus?
plan: List what Aaron actually devises, from the pit to the bargain for the hand, and note that he claims all of it.
Examine how Rome speaks of him: the word ‘black’ as insult, and its frequency.
Read 4.2 closely: ‘coal-black is better than another hue’ and the killing of the nurse to save the child.
Compare his refusal to repent with Tamora’s public pieties and Lucius’s ‘justice’.
Decide whether the play condemns him, admires him, or uses him to expose Rome, and whether those are exclusive.

essayQuestions.question: ‘A play in which revenge and justice cannot be told apart.’ How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Law, private revenge and the banquet
plan: Open with the failure of public justice: the forged letter, the condemned sons, the hanged clown, ‘Terras Astraea reliquit’.
Show how each revenge is staged in the forms of law or ceremony — a sacrifice, a trial, a banquet.
Use Tamora’s masque of Revenge to argue that the play knows its own genre and shows it being performed.
Consider whether Titus’s pie is justice by any standard the play offers.
Finish with Lucius, who calls his sentences ‘justice done’ and orders a woman’s body thrown to the birds.

discussionQuestions: Titus laughs when he is shown his sons’ heads. What is the laugh, and why does the play put it there rather than a speech?
Marcus speaks for forty lines over the mutilated Lavinia before helping her. Is the speech a failure of taste, or the point?
Aaron is the only character who protects a child. Does that change how we should read his confession?
Tamora’s plea for mercy in 1.1 is refused. If Titus had granted it, would there be a play?
Lucius ends the play ordering two more punishments. Has Rome learnt anything?

related.why: Shakespeare’s last Roman play, where the city again consumes the soldier who saved it, this time without a single death on stage until the end.
The revenge tragedy Shakespeare wrote a decade later, in which the revenger delays for four acts instead of plotting through them.
Gloucester’s blinding and Lear’s madness revisit the question this play asks first: how much can be done to a body on stage.
Written close in time, with another villain who takes the audience into his confidence and relishes his own designs.
Rome again, and a murder conducted as a ceremony by men who believe they are being pious.
